requirements.title: The processor character set includes both letter cases
requirements.source: 6.1.2 p3, second sentence (J3/24-007 PDF page 67, printed page 53, lines 17-18), using the p1-p2 letter list.
requirements.definition: The processor character set includes the upper-case and lower-case forms of all twenty-six listed letters. Inclusion of both forms is distinct from their equivalence outside character contexts. This does not prescribe an ASCII code value or the numerical relation between a lower-case letter and its upper-case counterpart.
requirements.oracle: A default-character value contains the twenty-six upper-case and twenty-six lower-case letters. Compare every pair of different positions by character equality and require distinct character values. All positions are within the initialized 52-character value. This detects collapse of two letters or of the two cases without assuming integer codes, code ordering, or any particular separation.
requirements.oracle_limitation: The finite oracle covers representability and distinctness of these 52 source characters in default character data, using the separately specified default-character and character-equality semantics. It does not inspect glyph style, processor input encoding, control characters, optional character kinds, or exhaustive collating-sequence constraints. No character-code conversion is used, so it does not assume that default integer can represent the size of the complete processor repertoire, as a default-kind ICHAR call would require. A successful program is not approval of the fixture.
requirements.dependencies: 6.1.2 p1-p2 defines the alphabet (PDF page 67). 7.4.4.2 p2-p3 supplies default character and the Fortran repertoire (PDF page 84); 7.4.4.3 p2-p4 gives literal kind and representable characters (PDF page 85). 10.1.5.5.1 p7-p8 defines character equality without depending on the collating order (PDF pages 180-181). The avoided character-code result-kind precondition is in 16.9.105 p5 (PDF page 419).

requirements.title: Letter case is equivalent outside character contexts
requirements.source: 6.1.2 p3, third sentence (J3/24-007 PDF page 67, printed page 53, lines 18-19).
requirements.definition: In program units, a lower-case letter is equivalent to the corresponding upper-case letter except within a character context. Under 3.21, character contexts are character literal constants and character string edit descriptors. The exception is not permission to fold the values of literals or output edit strings: their defining rules determine those values. Comment text has no effect under the separate source-form rules; it is not a third character context with an observable case-preservation effect.
requirements.oracle: Four independent programs separate the contexts. One declares all twenty-six one-letter identifiers in upper case, assigns distinct integers through lower-case uses, and reads them in upper case. Another mixes keyword and program/procedure-name case and checks a call's scalar result. The literal program uses both delimiter forms, checks corresponding character positions, and requires each upper/lower pair to differ, so folding both input and expected literals cannot produce a false pass. The FORMAT-statement program outputs both delimiter forms to initialized fixed-size internal records, checks IOSTAT before reading them, and checks exact positions and unequal case pairs.
requirements.oracle_limitation: This is a finite plan, not coverage of every keyword, operator, name context, source form, literal rule, or I/O operation. Character-context checks depend on 7.4.4.3 and 13.9 and are deliberately separate from the no-I/O name and literal cases. Neither a fixed ASCII case offset nor an ordering between the two cases is assumed. Comments are not given a fake preservation assertion. No negative program is inferred merely from this semantic equivalence rule.
requirements.dependencies: 3.21 (PDF page 21) defines both character contexts. 6.2.2/R603/C601 owns name grammar (PDF page 68). 6.3.1 p2 and 6.3.2.3 p1 (PDF pages 71-72) distinguish admissible comment characters from comments' lack of effect; fixed-form commentary is separately specified by 6.3.3.2 (PDF page 73). 7.4.4.3 p1-p5 supplies character literals (PDF pages 85-86). 13.3.2/R1322/C1313 and p5-p7 supplies edit-string syntax and its case exception (PDF page 292); 13.9 p1-p2 supplies output-only character-string editing (PDF page 307). Native character identity, not ASCII collation, follows from 7.4.4.4 p1 and 16.9.105 p5.

PDF page 67, lines 17-19: distinguish the letter syntax-class definition, both-case support, case equivalence, and its exact character-context boundary.
The listed set defines letter. Its use as an alphanumeric alternative is owned by R601; this class declaration is not a duplicate S requirement.

The equivalence rule excludes precisely the 3.21 character contexts: character literals and character string edit descriptors. Their value/output semantics remain in their defining clauses, not in a new local restriction on comments.
The three differently cased CALL statements illustrate the equivalence already required by p3. They add neither a new case-folding algorithm nor a separate call-syntax requirement.

review_rationale: Coordinator review independent of the draft authors; see doc/source_audits/lexical_batch_003.json. All 26 alphabet members, both required cases, equivalence outside the two exact character contexts, and the informative CALL example are accounted for. Direct character equality avoids an unnecessary integer-kind premise while preserving the finite repertoire oracle.
